subject: Analysis of data from a single point transect

messages.author: 5900eadecec2d82d
messages.subject: Analysis of data from a single point transect
parts:
Hi Cindy,

I'm cc'ing my answer to the list, so it will be there in the archives ready for
the next person who asks.

On Wed, 28 Jan 2004 23:45:26 -0400, Cindy Staicer wrote:

> >For some time I have been trying to figure out if DISTANCE can be
> >used to calculate a density for a given bird species at a SINGLE
> >point count. I have data for several species.

> >I have been working through the 2001 edition of Introduction to
> >Distance Sampling and the on-line manual, and I have searched the
> >archives but I haven't noticed an answer to my question.

Absolutely it can, just as it can from a single line transect (see the Ducknest
and Beercan example projects as examples).

There are two cases when you might want to do this:

The first is (as for the beercan example) when the surveyed strip *is* the whole
study area. This can happen for simulation exercises like the beercan study,
where they layed out cans in a strip 200 meters long and 40 meters wide (I think
that was it), and then surveyed a line down the middle with truncation distance
20 meters. You can think of the usual distance sampling estimator of abundance
as having two parts. First fit a detection function and use this to estimate the
average probabilty of detection within the strip (p). Use this to estimate the
number of animals in the surveyed area (as number seen divided by p). Second,
"scale up" this estimate to the number of animals in the whole study area. In
the case where the surveyed area *is* the study area you don't need the second
part. So the only source of uncertainty in the abundance estimate comes from
estimating the detection function. How do you tell this to Distance? One way
is under Model Definition | Variance | Encounter rate variance, click the option
to "Assume distribution is Poisson, with overdispersion factor" and then enter
0. This will give you no encounter rate variance -- what you want. I think
this is correct -- no doubt someone on the list will correct me if they
disagree. If you want a bootstrap estimate of variance, I guess the thing to do
is to bootstrap by observation.

The second case would be when you have a study area larger than your single
point or line, but for some reason your design was to have only one replicate.
Clearly, this is not a good design, but I have seen it on several occasions
(ideally, you'd like 20 or more lines or points). In this case, you do want
variation in encounter rate to enter the calculations. But you have only one
line, so the default option under Model Definition | Variance | Encounter rate
variance to "Estimate variance empirically" is not going to work (this uses the
between-line variation in encounter rate). So instead, you're going to have to
either assume the variation is Poisson (the second option), or Poisson with some
overdispersion (Buckland et al. 2001, page 242 cite Burnham et al. 1980 as
providing a rationale for values for overdispersion in the range 1.5-3 and in
the analysis of duck nest data (Table 8.4) got values around 1.7). Assuming
some number is not very satisfactory, as it will make a huge difference to the
final variance estimate and confidence limits, but you have no option. Using
temporal variation in encounter rate if you have repeat visits to the point will
certainly underestimate the variance.

Hope this helps,

- Len

messages.author: d718c6bb1db28db2
messages.subject: Re: Analysis of data from a single point transect
parts:
>> > >For some time I have been trying to figure out if DISTANCE can be
>> > >used to calculate a density for a given bird species at a SINGLE
>> > >point count. I have data for several species.

I would add two points to Len's response.

1. If the design comprises a single point, only in very unusual
circumstances would you get a large enough sample size to get an estimate
with reasonable precision. I can't envisage a real survey in which this
option would be useful. One reason for having many points, randomly
positioned (or a randomly-positioned grid of points) is that, on average,
the density of objects in the popn (whether detected or not) increases
linearly, as required. This is unlikely to be the case for a single
point, so that your estimate may be poor even if you have lots of
detections.

2. It is not clear from your query whether you really do have just one
point in your design, or whether you have many, but want to estimate
density separately for each point. In the latter case, you can select a
common detection function (or a common detection function model, but with
covariates that vary by point or object), but estimate density by sample
(point in this case). This can potentially be useful, but for most
species, you are likely to get an estimate of zero at many of the points.

Steve Buckland
